specs.note: wall & corner clearances: lettered table in the manual

steps: Unpack & inspect
Check the stove and parts for transit damage; the pack list is the stove, owner's manual and a bag of handles and hardware. Don't damage the label cable under the stove when lifting.
Choose the location
Freestanding room heater for a main living area, not a basement or confined space, and never in a factory-built fireplace. Check clearances to walls, floor, ceiling and chimney chase first.
Floor protection
Noncombustible floor protector under and beyond the stove: 48in x 36-3/4in minimum (US), 56in x 44in (Canada). No insulated hearth pad or R-value needed.
Set clearances
Wall and corner clearances come from the lettered table (Figure 4) for your connector type and heat shield. The door side stays 18" from the side wall unless the side door locking kit is installed.
Wall pass-through
Through a combustible wall, use a thimble or one of the four pass-through systems (A–D); the installation must conform to NFPA Code 211 or CAN/CSA-B365.

Where the connector passes through a wall or partition of combustible construction, the installation must conform to NFPA Code 211 or CAN/CSA-B365. A wall thimble is required through a combustible wall to a masonry chimney; a wall pass-through (chimney support package) when connecting to a prefabricated chimney.

  • A. Minimum 3.5in thick brick masonry, with at least 12in of brick from the clay liner to combustibles.
  • B. Solid-insulated, listed factory-built chimney length of the connector's inside diameter, 1in or more of insulation, minimum 9in air space to combustibles.
  • C. Minimum 24 gauge sheet steel connector with a ventilated 24 gauge thimble (two 1in air channels), separated from combustibles by at least 6in of glass fiber insulation.
  • D. Solid insulated, listed chimney length 2in larger inside than the connector, 1in or more of insulation, minimum 2in air space to combustibles; at least 12in long and spaced 1in from the connector.
Outside air (optional)
Kit 93-53500 to a minimum 3" duct; terminate no higher than the stove's air intake and screen it. Required in mobile homes; in Canada the stove must then be fastened to the floor.
Chimney connector
6" 24 or 25 MSG blued steel (or listed double wall), crimped ends toward the stove, three sheet metal screws per joint. Horizontal runs rise at least 1/4" per foot.

Use 6" diameter, 24 MSG or 25 MSG blued steel single wall pipe, or a listed double wall (rear) connector to reduce clearances. No aluminum or galvanized pipe, and never use stovepipe as a chimney.

  • Crimped end toward the stove, so creosote runs back into the stove.
  • Secure every joint, including the flue collar, with three sheet metal screws; #10 x 1/2" screws go into the pre-drilled flue collar holes.
  • As short and straight as possible; horizontal runs rise away from the stove at a minimum of 1/4" per foot.
  • Never through a floor, ceiling, attic or roof space, closet or similar concealed space.
  • Never into a flue used by another appliance, or into any air distribution duct.

Single wall clearances are generic; double wall clearances are specific to Simpson DuraVent DVL.
Chimney & draft
Listed Type HT (2100° F) chimney per UL 103 / ULC S629, or a lined, code-approved masonry chimney; 6" flue, not shared. Draft must be 0.06" to 0.1" WC; above 0.1" fit a stovepipe damper.

Connect to a listed Type HT (2100° F) chimney per UL 103 or ULC S629, or a code-approved masonry chimney with a flue liner. New installs need a 6" inside diameter flue; an existing 8" flue can be used with a reducer. An oversized flue builds creosote.

  • Chimney size: not less than the flue collar, nor more than three times its cross-sectional area.
  • Have a professional examine a masonry chimney and finish any repairs first; the cleanout door must seal tightly.
  • Choose an interior chimney where possible: it heats quickly and drafts better.
  • Buy the pass-through, T section, fire-stops, insulation shield, flashing and cap from the prefab chimney's maker.
  • Check the draft at installation: 0.06" to 0.1" WC. For drafts above 0.1" WC, install a stovepipe damper.
Mobile home (if applicable)
Per 24 CFR, Part 3280: outside air kit, stove fastened to the floor with the shipping clips, and a listed mobile home chimney kit. Never in a sleeping room.

• Install per 24 CFR, Part 3280 (HUD). An outside air kit must be used.
  • Permanently attach the stove to the floor with the shipping clips and fasteners long enough to reach the subfloor.
  • Mobile home chimney & connector kit to UL103 or ULC-S629, removable for transport: stainless spark arrester cap, storm collar, adjustable vented flashing (0/12 – 6/12), two 24" chimney pipes, 24" support box with built-in starter section and trim.
  • Chimney attached directly to the stove, at least 3 feet above the roof where it passes and 2 feet above any part of the home within 10 feet. Terminations removable at or below 13-1/2 feet above ground without special tools.
  • A wall exit 7 feet or less above ground needs a guard up to 7 feet.
  • Maintain the vapor barrier and the structural integrity of walls, floor, ceiling and roof.
Never install in a sleeping room. Remove the chimney when the home is transported. The front door stays closed except for start-up and loading.
Break-in & inspection
Build the first fire as a slow break-in fire (warm, not hot). Cool break-in flue gases can build creosote fast; inspect, and clean if needed, the stovepipe and chimney once break-in is done.

panels.title: Stove smokes
items: Operating technique → open the air control fully a minute before opening a door; bypass open first
Cold chimney or reverse draft → preheat the chimney; briefly open a window
Blocked chimney → check chimney and stovepipe for blockage or creosote
Oversized / undersized / too-short chimney → reline / draft inducer or replace / lengthen
Air infiltration → seal chimney connections and openings; check clean-out doors
Bypass not closed or catalysts not working → close bypass in the active range; inspect, brush or replace catalysts
Wrong fuel or another appliance on the flue → seasoned, dry cordwood; disconnect other appliances

panels.title: Back-puffing
items: Operating technique → air control fully open a minute before opening the door and a few minutes after reloading; bypass open
Extra low burn rate → burn at a higher rate
Chimney down-draft → install a chimney cap
Excessive ash build-up → empty the ash pan more often; avoid poor or green wood

panels.title: Uncontrolled or short burn
items: Unsealed or open door → close it tightly or replace the gaskets
Air leakage around the glass gasket → replace the gasket
Excessive draft → operate at low burn; draft over 0.1 wc needs stovepipe damper(s)
Extra long or oversized chimney → shorten it or add damper(s); reline
High winds or hilltop location → install a chimney cap

panels.title: Insufficient heat
items: Poor, low-Btu or green wood → air-dried wood, preferably dried at least one year
Low burn rate → operate at a higher burn rate
Cold exterior chimney → reline or insulate the chimney
Leaky stovepipe or chimney → insulated prefab system or properly sized masonry chimney
Too much heat loss from the house → insulation, efficient windows, caulking
Excessive ash build-up → empty the ash pan more often

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
Once the stove is broken in, this is the everyday start-up. Doors open with the handle turned clockwise; to latch, push the door in and turn the handle counterclockwise.

  1. Open the bypass handle (handle toward the back of the stove). Open the front or side door.
  2. Put five or six double sheets of tightly twisted newspaper in the center of the firebox. Lay about 10 pieces of kindling, 1/2" thick and 10" to 16" long, over it in a tee-pee.
  3. Open the primary air control fully: lever all the way left.
  4. Light the paper. Leave the front door slightly open until the kindling catches and the draft starts to pull. Never open the ash door to get a draft going.
  5. Close the door and let the fire burn.
  6. Add logs, small ones first, keeping them toward the center and away from the glass.
  7. When the catalyst thermometer shows Active, close the bypass and run on high for around 20 minutes.
  8. Set the burn rate with the air control: left for more heat, right for less.
Reloading: open the bypass first, then open the door a crack, pause, and open it fully so smoke clears. Reload on hot, red coals and run with the air fully open for 15 to 20 minutes. If the fire had burned down to charcoal, run medium to high for about 10 minutes so the catalysts reach about 600 °F before closing the bypass.

breakin.title: Break-in fires
breakin.html:
The soapstone has to be seasoned and the furnace cement cured slowly; over-firing a new stove can crack the soapstone. Build your first fire, and the first fire of every season, like this:

  1. Open the bypass. Put five or six double sheets of twisted newspaper in the center, with about ten pieces of kindling (1/2" thick, 10" to 16" long) crisscrossed over it.
  2. Open the air control fully (lever left) and light the paper. Leave the door slightly open only until the kindling catches, then close it.
  3. Keep a steady, low-heat fire, adding a few small chunks of wood at most. Aim for warm, not hot, to the touch. Steam, boiling moisture or hissing mean the soapstone is too hot.
  4. Once it's warm, close the air control so the fire dies out completely, and let the stove return to room temperature.
Note: the break-in steps say to close the air control by pushing it fully inward toward the stove (p. 23); the controls section says to move the lever right as far as possible for minimum air, and that it does not close completely (p. 20).

Smoke and smells are normal

First fires give off smoke and fumes as the paint and oils cure. Open a few windows; it usually fades after 10 to 20 minutes. If an odor persists, call your dealer. Break-in fires can dirty the glass and build creosote quickly, so have the stovepipe and chimney checked afterward.

bypass.title: The bypass & catalyst thermometer
bypass.html:
Your stove burns its smoke cleanly in a catalytic combustor. The bypass handle decides whether smoke goes through the catalyst or around it.

Handle toward the backBypass open: smoke goes around the catalyst
Handle toward the frontBypass closed: smoke goes through the catalyst

Open it

  • When you start a fire, until the catalyst heats up.
  • Every time, before you open the front door to load.

Close it

When the catalyst thermometer reads Active, close the bypass and keep it closed while the stove burns in that range. If it reads Inactive, open the bypass until the stove heats up. Closing it too soon can let fly ash build up on the catalysts.

Too Hot? Keep the door closed, fully close the air control, and let the stove cool until the thermometer is back in Active.

The catalyst becomes active around 500 °F, and the stove typically runs between 800 °F and 1300 °F. With the catalyst working you should see little to no smoke from the chimney.

air.title: Air control & burn rates
air.html:
The primary air lever sits under the ash lip. More air gives a faster, hotter burn; less air a slower, cooler one. It never closes completely, and small moves at the low end make a big difference.

LowLever all the way right
Medium lowFrom low, a little less than 1/16" left
Medium highFrom low, about 3/8" left
HighLever all the way left

Medium low is the typical setting and the best choice when the stove is unattended. Long stretches on low build creosote, so check the chimney more often if you burn low a lot. Run it on high once or twice a day for 35 to 45 minutes to heat the stovepipe and chimney.

Don't over-fire. Signs include warped parts, short burn times, a roaring sound in the stove or stovepipe, and a discolored stovepipe. If you suspect it, stop using the stove and call your dealer immediately. Signs of over-firing void the warranty.

The minimum low burn rate is set at the factory and must not be altered.

wood.title: What wood to burn
wood.html:
Burn only natural firewood (cordwood). The stove isn't designed for other fuels. Build the fire right on the firebox floor, with no grate.

Dry wood matters most

  • Season green wood: split it, stack it, and let it air-dry for a year.
  • Seasoned wood is typically at or near 20% moisture; a hand-held moisture meter will tell you.
  • Green wood may give less than 2000 Btu per pound; dry wood up to 7000 Btu per pound.
  • Stack it on skids or blocks and cover only the top. Tarps over the sides trap moisture.

Softwoods burn hotter and faster; hardwoods burn longer and make better coals. Air-dried, seasoned hardwoods give higher efficiency and lower emissions.

Never burn coal, charcoal, pellets, artificial or wax logs, kiln-dried, painted, treated or pressure treated wood, unseasoned wood, plywood, particleboard, cardboard, paper products (including colored or glossy paper), garbage or trash, lawn clippings, materials containing rubber (including tires), materials containing plastic, waste petroleum products, paints or paint thinners, solvents, flammable fluids, asphalt products, materials containing asbestos, construction or demolition debris, railroad ties, driftwood (including salt water driftwood) or other previously salt water saturated materials, or manure or animal remains. Burning these materials may release toxic fumes, make the stove ineffective and cause smoke. Burn untreated wood only: other materials such as wood preservatives, metal foils, coal, plastic, garbage, sulfur or oil may damage the catalysts. Never use gasoline, kerosene or lighter fluid to start or freshen a fire. Fire starters made of paper, cardboard, sawdust or wax are fine for lighting.

Don't store firewood within the stove's clearances, and don't load ice-covered wood into a burning stove.

ash.title: Emptying the ashes
ash.html:
Empty the ashes at the end of every week, sooner if the firebox is full. You can leave a thin layer in the firebox.

Using the ash pan

  1. Let the fire die down to dead coals. The ash pan gets hot, so it's best to remove it after the stove cools.
  2. Open the ash door: grip its handle from the bottom, rotate it toward you, then pull it away from the stove and lower it until it hangs.
  3. With the pan in place, pull the ash grate handle toward you, or move it in and out, to sift ash into the pan.
  4. Grip the ash pan handle and pull the pan out.

Don't let ash build up around the door openings. It can spill out or pack into the gasket channel and spoil the seal.

Disposal: put ashes straight into a metal container with a tight-fitting lid. Don't add trash or pour in water. Set it on a noncombustible floor or the ground outside, never on a combustible surface or vinyl flooring, and away from anything that burns. Keep it closed until all coals are cool; they can stay hot for several days. Never use wooden or plastic containers, trash cans or bags.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
The window is a tough ceramic, not plain glass. Clean it only when the fire is out and the glass is cool.

  1. Dip a damp paper towel in gray ash.
  2. Rub the inside of the glass in a circular motion until the deposits are gone.
  3. Clean up with window cleaner or a commercial stove glass cleaner, following its instructions. Wipe it off with a soft cloth or black-and-white newsprint.
Note: p. 29 suggests finishing with window cleaner or a commercial stove glass cleaner, then says to use only a cleaner made specifically for woodstoves.
  • Never use a razor blade, steel wool or anything abrasive. Scratches weaken the glass.
  • Glass that's always dirty means the fire runs too cool or the wood is wet.
  • A hot fire burns residue off: after closing the bypass, run on high for around 20 minutes.
  • Don't use the stove with cracked or broken glass, and don't slam the door. Replacement glass comes from your dealer, and only a qualified service person should fit it.

care.title: Upkeep checklist
care.html:
Every week

  • Empty the ashes, sooner if the firebox is full.

Every other month

  • Look over the chimney connector and chimney for creosote.
  • Do the dollar bill test: with the stove cool, shut the door on a dollar bill. If it pulls out with no resistance, the door isn't sealing. Adjust the latch or change the door gasket.
  • Check the face of the catalytic combustor for fly ash and soot, and brush it off with a soft-bristled brush. Look at it at least 3 times a heating season.

End of every season

  • Take the chimney connector apart and clean it; replace pieces showing rust or wear.
  • Inspect the chimney and clean it if needed.
  • Clean out the inside of the stove, and check and clean the catalytic combustor.
  • Replace door gasket that's worn, frayed, cracked or very hard.
Creosote: check daily for build-up until experience shows how often you need to clean to be safe. If more than 1/4" builds up, have it removed. A certified chimney sweep is recommended, with a professional inspection of the whole system before each heating season. Plan on new door gasket every two to three seasons.

safety.title: Chimney fire & everyday safety
safety.html:
If you have a stovepipe or chimney fire

  1. If the fire is too threatening, leave and call the fire department right away. If not, go on:
  2. Close the primary air control.
  3. Close the stovepipe damper, if you have one.
  4. Close the bypass damper.
  5. Keep the front door closed.
Never throw water on the stove, stovepipe or chimney during a chimney fire. The extreme heat makes instant steam that can cause serious harm.

Once it's out, leave the air control and bypass closed and let the fire die out completely. Inspect the stove, stovepipe and chimney, and correct any damage before you use the stove again.

Everyday safety

  • Keep furniture, drapes, clothing and other combustibles at least 36" from the stove.
  • It's hot while burning: keep children and pets away.
  • Fit smoke and CO detectors throughout the home, and keep a fire extinguisher rated "A B C" handy.
  • Keep the doors closed while it burns, and keep flammable liquids well away.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
Hearthstone covers defects in material or workmanship for the original retail purchaser only, on a stove installed by an authorized Hearthstone dealer or their representative. It isn't transferable. "Limited Lifetime" means 10 years.

Stone; cast iron not listed elsewhereLimited Lifetime
Door handles and latches; steel components and firebox5 years
Appliance electrical and gas components2 years
Enamel finish, accessories, glass, all other components1 year

Rows checked for only some fuel types (such as baffles and the ash grate) are in the grid on this page. Dealer labor is paid in year one only if a dealer installed the stove.

Catalysts are covered by Applied Ceramics: free replacement if one stops working within two (2) years, then a prorated price from $130 (year 3) to $160 (year 6).

Note: the same catalyst warranty also refers to one replacement per defective catalyst returned "during the three year period" (p. 36).
Note: the warranty grid covers glass for 1 year (p. 37), but the exclusions list glass among wear parts that aren't covered (p. 38).

Not covered: over-firing, the wrong fuel, or installation not per the manual and codes. Claims go through your Hearthstone dealer.

specOutput.title: Heat output, efficiency & emissions
specOutput.html:
Maximum heat output75,000 BTUs per hour of cordwood
EPA test output14000 to 33000 Btu
Weighted efficiency78% (HHV)
Particulate emissions0.65 g/hr.
Heated areaUp to a maximum of 2,400 square feet

The two output figures measure different things: 75,000 BTUs per hour is the maximum heat output burning cordwood, based on independent laboratory tests (p. 7); 14000 to 33000 Btu (output) is the range the stove delivered under the specific EPA test conditions, which use crib wood (p. 2).

Certified to the EPA 2020 particulate emissions standard using crib wood (EPA Method 28R); p. 2 writes the rate as 0.65 gr/hr. Efficiency is the weighted average across the 4 burn rate categories (EPA Method 28R and CSA B415-10). CO by category 1 to 4: 40.46, 37.04, 63.46 and 79.04 g/hr.

The manufacturer-set minimum low burn rate must not be altered. Insulation, windows, floor plan, stove placement and fuel quality may limit the area heated.

specFirebox.title: Firebox & fuel
specFirebox.html:
Firebox capacity2.45 cubic feet
Maximum log lengthUp to 24", through side door
Burn timeUp to 30+ hrs. (Heat Life: up to 30 hours)

Wood per cubic foot of firebox varies from 10 to 25 lbs. depending on type of wood, moisture content and packing density. Natural cordwood only, burned directly on the firebox floor with no grate. Loads through the front or side door.

specDims.html:

The dimension drawing (Figure 1) is on this page. The label hangs on a cable under the stove: don't damage it when lifting, and store it in the holding clip on the bottom shield after final positioning.

specFlue.title: Connector, chimney & draft
specFlue.html:
Connector6" diameter, 24 MSG or 25 MSG blued steel
Metal chimney6" inside diameter, Type HT (2100° F), UL 103 / ULC S629
Masonry chimney6" round or 8" x 8" square flue, lined
Existing flue8" diameter with a reducer
Draft0.06" to 0.1" WC

Chimney size: not less than the flue collar, nor more than three times its cross-sectional area. Liner: UL 1777 or ULC S635. Never shared with another appliance or connected to an air distribution duct.

No aluminum or galvanized pipe. Double wall (rear) connector options include Simpson Dura Vent DVL and Metalbestos DS; Security, GSW and Ameritec are also acceptable. A stovepipe damper is generally not needed, but install one for drafts above 0.1" WC (some installs need more than one). Check the draft at installation.

specHeight.title: Chimney height & construction
specHeight.html:
Top exit, recommended min.16 feet off the floor (13 feet 5 1/8 inches from top of stove)
Rear exit, recommended min.19 feet off the floor (16 feet 5 1/8 inches from top of stove)
Recommended max.30 feet
Above roof openingAt least 3 feet
Above roof within 10 feetAt least 2 feet

The chimney must be long enough for the minimum draft (0.06" to 0.1" water column); use a damper where the required height gives too much draft.

Interior chimney: at least 2" to combustibles, fire stops at floors and ceilings, insulation at least 2" away. Exterior chimney: at least 1" to combustibles. Masonry walls (4" mortared brick or block, or rubble/stone) must use a liner: tile with 5/8" minimum wall and 1" air space, or UL listed 6" stainless. Spark arrester openings must not pass a sphere larger than 1/2 inch and must pass a 3/8 inch sphere. Height and configuration diagrams are Figures 8 and 9.

specFloor.title: Floor protection
specFloor.html:
US minimum48in x 36-3/4in
Canada minimum56in x 44in
Insulated hearth padNot required; no R-value requirement

On a combustible floor, a noncombustible floor protector goes under the stove and extends beyond it, for example a continuous layer of tile, brick, slate, glass or another noncombustible facing. How it is positioned around the stove is shown only in the hearth drawing (Figure 3) on this page.

Some LVP and LVT flooring begins to warp at 110° Fahrenheit. Check the flooring maker's maximum temperature; additional shielding may be needed.

specClear.title: Clearances to combustibles
specClear.html:
Door side to side wall18" unless the side door locking kit is installed
Furniture, drapes, other combustibles36"
Min. alcove width62.25"
Max. alcove depth52"
Min. alcove ceiling, single wall connector68"
Min. alcove ceiling, double wall connector61.5"

Wall and corner clearances (A to E) are tabled for four set-ups: single or double wall connector, each with or without the close clearance heat shield (kit #93-68600). The letters are defined only in the drawing (Figure 4), so read them on this page. Connector clearances by vertical pipe length before the elbow (Figure 5) and trim and mantle clearances (Figure 6) are also drawings.

Double wall clearances are specific to Simpson DuraVent DVL; check your connector maker's specs. An NFPA 211 wall protection system approved by the authority having jurisdiction can reduce clearances. Leave room to load through the side door.

specAir.title: Outside air & kits
specAir.html:
Outside air kit93-53500

The kit attaches to the underside of the stove. The IRC doesn't allow the duct to terminate higher than the appliance; Hearthstone recommends the same level as the air intake or lower. Keep it clear of snow and leaves, screen it with 1/4" x 1/4" mesh and fit a rain/wind proof hood. Required in all mobile home installs. In Canada, a stove on outside air must be fastened to the floor with the shipping clips.

conflicts.issue: Closing the primary air control: break-in step 6 says to close it by pushing it fully inward toward the stove (p. 23); the controls section says move the lever right as far as possible for minimum airflow and that it does not close completely (p. 20; also everyday step 8 on p. 23 and LOW BURN on p. 24).

Heat output: maximum heat output 75,000 BTUs per hour of cordwood (p. 7) vs 14000 to 33000 Btu (output) under EPA test conditions with crib wood (p. 2). Different test bases, but two different output figures.
conflicts.reason: Different measurements, each labelled in the manual: 75,000 BTUs per hour is the maximum heat output burning cordwood from independent laboratory tests (p. 7); 14000 to 33000 Btu (output) is the range delivered under the specific EPA test conditions with crib wood (p. 2). Both fit; the drawer now says what each figure is.

conflicts.issue: Glass kit part number: 'Required Glass Kit: Part Number: 90-58901' (p. 28) vs '93-58300 GLASS KIT' in the optional accessories list (p. 33).
Glass cleaner: 'clean up with window cleaner or with commercial stove glass cleaners' vs 'Use a cleaner specifically manufactured for woodstoves only' (both p. 29).

Catalyst warranty: free replacement if it ceases to function within two (2) years, prorated years 3-6, but also 'one replacement catalyst for each defective catalyst returned during the three year period' (p. 36).
Glass coverage: the warranty grid lists Glass at 1 Year for all fuel types (p. 37); exclusion 3 lists glass among wear parts not covered (p. 38).

Creosote check frequency: 'Check daily for creosote build-up until experience shows how often you need to clean to be safe' (p. 6) vs inspecting the chimney connector and chimney every other month (p. 6 checklist; 'at least once every two months', p. 29).
conflicts.reason: The daily check applies until experience shows how often you need to clean; the every-other-month inspection is the minimum the manual sets (p. 29: 'at least once every two months'). Both fit, and the drawer shows both.

review.notes: Not transcribed (figure-only or ambiguous in the text): the wall/corner clearance values A-E on p. 10 are keyed to letters defined only in Figure 4, so the guide links the page instead (the catalog clearances_note's side 18"/rear 16"/corner 9" and side 16"/rear 6"/corner 9" do equal the A/B/E columns of the single-wall-no-shield and double-wall-with-shield rows, but the letter meanings can't be confirmed from text); Figure 5 connector clearances (p. 11) have interleaved column headers, so with/without heat shield values can't be assigned; Figure 3 hearth layout (p. 9), Figure 6 trim and mantle clearances (p. 13), Figures 8-9 chimney diagrams (pp. 16-17), Figure 20 acceptable catalyst distortion (p. 27) and the safety label (p. 34, no text) are drawings only. Warranty grid (p. 37): only rows checked in all three fuel columns were transcribed; rows with one or two checks (clean burning air supply system, burner and logs, burn pot and baffles, refractory/vermiculite panels/baffles, ash grate) can't be assigned to a fuel from the text. p. 2 writes the particulate rate as '0.65 gr/hr.', p. 7 as '0.65 g/hr.' (guide uses g/hr and mentions the p. 2 wording). p. 21 says unauthorized fuel such as coal could produce high levels of 'carbon dioxide'; p. 18 says other fuels could generate dangerous levels of carbon monoxide; the guide only says such fuels aren't safe. Emergency procedure (p. 6) says 'perform the next three steps' but lists four; the guide lists all four. Kindling 10" to 16" is given as 254-457 mm (break-in) and 254-406 mm (everyday) on p. 23; guide uses inches only. Reloading: p. 29 says run fully open 15 to 20 minutes after reloading; p. 23 says about 10 minutes at medium to high when rekindling a cool or charcoal-stage fire; both are given in the light drawer. Broken cross-references in the manual: p. 6 'Refer to page Error! Bookmark not defined.'; p. 18 outside air 'See page 12' (section is on p. 13); p. 14 spark arrester 'See page 17' (text on p. 16); p. 27 catalyst warranty 'page 35' (text on p. 36) and 'Figure 17'/'Figure 18' (Figures 20/21); p. 16 'SEE FIGURE 9' for chimney height (Figure 8); p. 19 controls 'See Figure 10' (Figure 12). The manual calls the stove catalytic throughout; 'hybrid' appears only in the generic phrase 'This catalytic (or hybrid) heater' (p. 26), so the catalog's combustion_type 'hybrid' was not listed as a mismatch. Blower kit 93-57600 is listed but the manual has no blower operating instructions, so there is no blower tile. Catalog features not confirmed by the manual text: 'rear heat shield included' (pack list on p. 8 is stove, owner's manual, bag of handles and hardware; parts list shows a top heat shield 5360-085) and 'side-loading door on the left' (the door side isn't stated in the text). Cover notes a French manual is available online; no French-only or scrambled text in this file. No code tables, so codes is empty.
